topic: Myth: crop sensors give you more zoom / reach. Same lens = same image; a smaller sensor only records the middle. Real reach = pixels on subject (pixel density).

youtube.title: Your Crop Sensor Isn't Zooming In (Crop Factor Myth)
youtube.description:
A crop sensor doesn't magnify anything. A lens projects the same image no matter which camera is behind it; a smaller sensor just records a smaller central part of it.
Crop factors: ~1.5x for Nikon DX, Sony and Fujifilm APS-C (23.5 x 15.6 mm), 1.6x for Canon APS-C (22.3 x 14.9 mm), 2x for Micro Four Thirds, vs 36 x 24 mm full frame. So a 50 mm lens on APS-C gives the field of view of a ~75 mm lens (~80 mm on Canon) on full frame - same focal length, no extra magnification.
The only real 'reach' is pixels on the subject: cropping a 24 MP full-frame image to the APS-C area leaves about 24/1.5^2 = 10.7 MP (9.4 MP at 1.6x), while a 24 MP APS-C sensor puts all 24 MP there (~2.25x the pixels on the bird). The visuals are a real numpy simulation: one analytic lens image sampled by both sensors at their real pixel pitches (6.0 um vs 3.9 um).
Sources: Wikipedia 'Crop factor' and 'APS-C'; Roger Clark, clarkvision.com 'Crop factor and telephoto reach'; J. Polak, 'The mathematics of reach'.
